624.title: Verses of trust (Isaiah 12:2)
624.hook: Havdalah opens with "Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust"
624.howItsDone: Havdalah is said after nightfall on Saturday, at home or in synagogue: opening verses of trust, then blessings over wine, fragrant spices and a multi-wicked candle, and the blessing of separation; everyone joins in the line from Esther and responds 'so may it be for us'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the long Shabbat afternoon, with Pirkei Avot and psalms. Your line was if not now, when. Today, the stars come out, and Shabbat ends.

Saturday night. Three stars are out. Somewhere a family is standing in a dim kitchen. Someone holds a braided candle with several wicks, burning like a small torch. A cup of wine is filled to the brim, spilling over a little onto the plate. A box of spices is passed from hand to hand. This is Havdalah, separation, the short ceremony that ends Shabbat. And before any blessing is said, before the wine or the fire, the first thing the family says is a line about not being afraid.
screen: `THREE STARS ARE OUT.` → `A BRAIDED CANDLE, A FULL CUP.` → `FIRST: DON'T BE AFRAID.`

segments.voice: Havdalah begins with a handful of verses, mostly from Isaiah and the Psalms. The first, in the old Jewish translation, is Isaiah 12: "Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid." And the next: "Therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation." Why start the end of Shabbat with trust? Think about what's happening. For a day, there were no requests, no work, no money, no errands. Shabbat was a shelter. Now the week is about to come back, with everything it carries. So before you step out, you say: I will trust, and will not be afraid. Then a few more verses of the same kind, and the last one is from the book of Esther, about a moment when danger turned to rescue: "The Jews had light and gladness, and joy and honour." At that line, in many homes, everyone says together: so may it be for us. Then the four blessings. Over the wine. Over the spices: tradition says each person is given an extra soul on Shabbat, the one we met in V'shamru, and the fragrance comforts us as it leaves. Over the fire, the first light kindled after Shabbat, which a midrash connects to Adam, who discovered fire as the very first Shabbat ended. And then the blessing of separation itself: blessed is the one who separates holy from ordinary, light from darkness, the seventh day from the six days of work. The week begins. But it begins with trust said first.
screen: `I WILL TRUST, AND NOT BE AFRAID.` · `THE WELLS OF SALVATION.` · `SO MAY IT BE FOR US.` · `WINE, SPICES, FIRE, SEPARATION.` · then, large: `I WILL TRUST.`

segments.voice: Name to yourself the one thing in the week ahead you're most nervous about. Then say, slowly, aloud or inside: I will trust, and will not be afraid. You don't have to feel it fully; Havdalah says it first, as a way to begin.
Havdalah, the short ceremony that ends Shabbat, which opens with verses of trust: I will trust, and will not be afraid.
Your line: I will trust. One braided candle, and the week begins. See you tomorrow.

625.title: Elijah, come soon
625.hook: after Havdalah, a song for Elijah, who is to announce redemption
625.howItsDone: Eliyahu HaNavi is sung at the end of Havdalah on Saturday night in many homes and synagogues; Elijah also has a cup at the Passover seder and a chair at a brit milah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Havdalah, which opens with verses of trust. Your line was I will trust. Today, the song that comes right after the candle goes out.

The Havdalah candle is dipped into the spilled wine, and it goes out with a hiss. The room is darker now. Shabbat is over. And then the room starts singing about a man whose death the Bible never records. Eliyahu hanavi. Elijah the prophet. It's the same Elijah we met on Mount Carmel, calling down fire in the afternoon. But here he's not a figure from a story. He's someone the song asks to show up, soon, maybe this very week.
screen: `THE CANDLE HISSES OUT.` → `A MAN WHOSE DEATH IS NEVER RECORDED.` → `MAYBE THIS VERY WEEK.`

segments.voice: First, why no death? In the book of Kings, Elijah doesn't die the way others do. He's walking with his student Elisha, and a chariot of fire and horses of fire come between them, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind into heaven. The text never records his death. So in Jewish tradition, he's still around. Then the promise. The closing verses of the prophets in the Hebrew Bible, in Malachi, say, in the old Jewish translation: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and terrible day of the LORD." And he will turn the hearts of parents to children, and the hearts of children to their parents. So in Jewish tradition Elijah becomes the one who announces redemption, the herald who comes before the messiah. The song is simple. Elijah the prophet, Elijah the Tishbite, Elijah the Gileadite. May he come to us soon, in our days, with the messiah, son of David. Why sing it on Saturday night? There's a tradition, built on a discussion in the Talmud, that Elijah won't arrive on Shabbat itself. Once Shabbat ends, the door is open again. So the song is a kind of hope at the start of the week: maybe this week. Elijah shows up all over Jewish life. A cup is filled for him at the Passover seder, and the door is opened. A chair is set for him at a baby boy's circumcision. In folk stories he appears in disguise, a beggar, a stranger, to help someone in trouble.

segments.voice: Malachi says Elijah will turn the hearts of parents and children toward each other. Think of one relationship where a heart could turn, and without planning anything, picture this week bringing one small turn: a call returned, a kind word, a door opened.

626.title: Praise on the festivals
626.hook: the Hallel psalms are sung after the Amidah on festivals and new moons
626.howItsDone: Hallel (Psalms 113–118) is sung after the morning Amidah on Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret, Shavuot, the first day or days of Passover and Hanukkah; a shortened half Hallel is said on Rosh Chodesh and the last days of Passover, and none is said on Rosh Hashanah or Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eliyahu HaNavi, the song for Elijah as Shabbat ends. Your line was the door is open again. Today, from Shabbat to the festivals, and the psalms they sing.

Here's a Hebrew word that has traveled far: hallelujah. It's in hymns, gospel songs, a famous chorus by Handel, a famous song by Leonard Cohen. It means praise God, hallelu-Yah. Take the first half, hallel, praise, and make it the name of a set of psalms. On the festivals, they're sung right after the morning Amidah, often with the whole room joining in. On some days, the room sings all of them. On others, it deliberately skips a few.
screen: `HALLELUJAH: PRAISE GOD.` → `HALLEL: A SET OF PSALMS.` → `SOME DAYS, A FEW ARE SKIPPED.`

segments.voice: Hallel is Psalms 113 through 118, six psalms sung together. Near its start, in the old Jewish translation: "From the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof the LORD'S name is to be praised." And it includes this line, from Psalm 118: "This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it." It's sung on Sukkot, on Shavuot, at the start of Passover, and on all eight days of Hanukkah. Those are full Hallel days. Then there's half Hallel, where parts of two psalms are left out. That's for the new moon each month, and for the last days of Passover. Why only half on the end of Passover? A later explanation draws on a story from the Talmud. When the Egyptians were drowning in the sea, the angels wanted to sing, and God stopped them: the work of my hands is drowning, and you want to sing? So on those days, the joy is real but held back. Even a victory has a cost. And on the Days of Awe, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, there's no Hallel at all. The Talmud gives the reason as a picture: the King sits on the throne of judgment, with the books of life and death open before him. Is this the moment to sing? So Hallel tracks the mood of the calendar. Full joy, partial joy, and the days when praise goes quiet out of awe.
screen: `PSALMS 113 TO 118.` · `THIS IS THE DAY.` · `HALF HALLEL: JOY HELD BACK.` · `NONE ON THE DAYS OF JUDGMENT.` · then, large: `PRAISE ON THE HOLIDAYS.`

segments.voice: Take one line: this is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it. If prayer isn't yours, try: this is the day; I'll be glad in it. Say it once plainly, then sing it to any tune that comes, a little louder than feels normal, and sit in the quiet after the sound.
Hallel. Praise: Psalms 113 to 118, sung in full on joyful days, in part on some, and not at all on the Days of Awe.

627.title: Remembering
627.hook: a memorial prayer on Yom Kippur and the last days of festivals
627.tomorrow: Who by fire, who by water
627.howItsDone: Yizkor is said in Ashkenazi synagogues on Yom Kippur, Shemini Atzeret, the last day of Passover and the second day of Shavuot (outside Israel); each person inserts the names of those they remember and often pledges charity, and many with living parents step out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hallel, praise that rises and falls with the calendar. Your line was praise on the holidays. Today, a quieter moment on the same festivals.

It's the last day of a festival. The synagogue is fuller than usual. Then the rabbi announces Yizkor, and something unusual happens. A handful of people, often younger ones, stand up and walk out. Not rudely. Quietly, as if on cue. They'll wait in the hallway and come back in a few minutes. The people who stay have someone to remember. Inside, the room gets very still. People hold small prayer books close to their faces. Some are crying. Some just stare at a name.
screen: `A FEW PEOPLE WALK OUT.` → `THOSE WHO STAY.` → `STARING AT A NAME.`

segments.voice: Yizkor means may he remember. The prayer begins: may God remember the soul of my father, or my mother, or my husband, my wife, my child, my friend, and the listener fills in the name. In Ashkenazi communities it's said four times a year: on Yom Kippur, and on the last day of Passover, of Shavuot, and of Sukkot, at Shemini Atzeret. Each time, in the middle of a festival, the community stops to remember. Where did it come from? Some historians trace it to the Rhineland, in the time of the Crusades, when whole Jewish communities were killed. Survivors kept memorial books with the names of the dead, and read them aloud. What began as remembering martyrs became remembering everyone. Many Sephardi communities have their own memorial prayers, called hashkavah, said at other times. Part of Yizkor, for many, is a promise to give charity in the person's memory. The idea is that the living can do good on someone's behalf, so that their life keeps doing good. And then there's the custom you saw in the hook. In many communities, people whose parents are living leave the room during Yizkor. Some say it's to avoid tempting fate by standing among mourners. Others say it's out of kindness, to give the bereaved privacy. It's a folk custom, not a law, and plenty of people stay to remember others. And some prayer books add a prayer for the Jews killed in the Holocaust, for whom no one else may be left to say a name.
screen: `YIZKOR: MAY HE REMEMBER.` · `FOUR TIMES A YEAR.` · `MEMORIAL BOOKS FROM THE RHINELAND.` · `A PROMISE OF CHARITY.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THEM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has died, a parent, a grandparent, a friend, a teacher, even someone you never met but carry, and say their name out loud, once. Then picture one ordinary thing about them, their hands, their laugh, the way they said your name, and stay with it.
Yizkor. May he remember. The memorial prayer said on Yom Kippur and the last days of the festivals, with a name filled in by each person.
Your line: remember them. Their names are still worth saying, out loud. See you tomorrow.

628.title: Who by fire, who by water
628.hook: the High Holy Day prayer that ends: return, prayer and giving soften the decree
628.howItsDone: Unetaneh Tokef is chanted in the repetition of the Musaf Amidah on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur in Ashkenazi congregations, with the ark often open; the congregation says aloud the closing line about teshuvah, tefillah and tzedakah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yizkor, and the names said aloud in the middle of the festival. Your line was remember them. Today, a prayer of the High Holy Days, and the line a whole congregation answers with.

A shepherd stands at the gate of the fold, counting the flock. Each sheep passes under his staff, one at a time, and he looks at each one. That's the image at the heart of a prayer said on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. Every living being passing, one by one, before God. And then the prayer starts listing what might happen to each of us this coming year. It's a list that makes a room go very still. A singer once turned it into a famous song called Who by Fire.
screen: `A SHEPHERD COUNTING THE FLOCK.` → `ONE BY ONE, UNDER THE STAFF.` → `A LIST THAT STOPS THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Unetaneh tokef means let us declare the power, the power of the holiness of this day. It describes a heavenly court. A great shofar is sounded, and a still, small voice is heard. Even the angels tremble. The book of memories is opened, and each person's signature is in it. Then the famous lines. On Rosh Hashanah it is written, and on Yom Kippur it is sealed. How many will pass away, and how many be born. Who will live, and who will die. Who in their time, and who before their time. Who by fire, and who by water. Who by sword, who by beast, who by hunger, who by thirst. Who will rest, and who will wander. Who will be poor, and who will be rich. It's hard to hear, especially for anyone who has lost someone. And then the whole congregation answers, often loudly, with the line the whole prayer turns on: but teshuvah, tefillah and tzedakah. Return, prayer and righteous giving. They make the evil of the decree pass. Notice the wording. Not they cancel the decree. They soften its evil, its harshness. People have read that many ways. Some say these three can change what happens. Others say they change how we meet what happens. There's a medieval story that Rabbi Amnon of Mainz composed this prayer as he was dying, a martyr. But texts found in the Cairo Geniza suggest the prayer is older than him. The story may be legend. The prayer is older than the legend.
screen: `LET US DECLARE THE POWER.` · `WRITTEN, THEN SEALED.` · `WHO BY FIRE, WHO BY WATER.` · `BUT RETURN, PRAYER, GIVING.` · then, large: `TESHUVAH, TEFILLAH, TZEDAKAH.`

segments.voice: Hold each of the three in mind for a few breaths: teshuvah, returning to a better way; tefillah, prayer, or simply honest words; tzedakah, giving to someone who needs it. Notice which one is calling you today, an apology, a few honest words, a gift, and let it settle.
Unetaneh tokef. Let us declare the power. The High Holy Day prayer of who by fire, who by water, answered by return, prayer and giving.
Your line: teshuvah, tefillah, tzedakah. Return, prayer and giving soften the harshness of the decree. Day six hundred twenty-eight, done.

629.title: Our father, our king
629.hook: a litany of requests in the Days of Awe
629.carry: we have no king but you
629.howItsDone: Avinu Malkeinu is said after the Amidah during the Ten Days of Repentance, from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, and on public fast days, usually with the ark open; it is generally omitted on Shabbat, and its last line is often sung together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Unetaneh Tokef: who by fire, who by water, and the three things that soften the decree. Your line was teshuvah, tefillah, tzedakah. Today, two words that sit side by side.

A drought in the land of Israel, nearly two thousand years ago. A public fast is called. A great sage stands before the ark and says the long, proper prayers, blessing after blessing. No rain. Then his student steps up. He doesn't say a long prayer. He says a few short lines, each beginning with the same two words, words that don't quite fit together. And the Talmud says: the rain came down.
screen: `A DROUGHT, A PUBLIC FAST.` → `THE LONG PRAYERS: NO RAIN.` → `TWO WORDS THAT DON'T FIT.`

segments.voice: The sage was Rabbi Eliezer. The student was Rabbi Akiva. And the two words were avinu malkeinu: our father, our king. The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, gives his words: our father, our king, we have no king but you. Our father, our king, for your sake, have mercy on us. That was the seed. Over the centuries, more lines were added, until the prayer became a long litany, in the Ashkenazi rite more than forty lines, each starting the same way. Our father, our king, inscribe us in the book of good life. Our father, our king, renew for us a good year. Our father, our king, hear our voice. It's said during the ten Days of Awe, from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, and on public fast days. But why those two words together? A father is close. You can climb into his lap. A king is far. You approach him with care, and he can judge you. The prayer refuses to choose. God is both: the one who loves you like a parent and the one who holds you to account like a ruler. Some people find the father easier to pray to; some find the king. The prayer makes you hold both in the same breath, line after line. And then the last line, which many congregations sing slowly, together: our father, our king, be gracious to us and answer us, for we have no deeds; deal with us in righteousness and kindness, and save us. After all the requests, an admission: we don't have enough to show. Answer us anyway.
screen: `RABBI AKIVA IN A DROUGHT.` · `A LITANY OF REQUESTS.` · `CLOSE AS A FATHER, FAR AS A KING.` · `WE HAVE NO DEEDS; ANSWER US.` · then, large: `OUR FATHER, OUR KING.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say avinu malkeinu, or in English, our father, our king, once, very slowly: feel the first word come close, and the second step back. If prayer isn't yours, think of someone who was both tender and demanding with you, a parent, a coach, a teacher, and hold both sides of them at once.
Avinu malkeinu. Our father, our king. Rabbi Akiva's words in a drought, grown into the litany of the Days of Awe.
Your line: we have no king but you. Close and far, in the same breath. Until tomorrow.

630.title: We have sinned
630.hook: the Yom Kippur confessions are in the plural: all of us together
630.howItsDone: Ashamnu and Al Chet are said in every Amidah of Yom Kippur, and in the repetition by the congregation together, each person lightly striking the chest at each sin; many communities also say Ashamnu in weekday prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Avinu Malkeinu, close as a father, high as a king. Your line was we have no king but you. Today, the confession at the center of Yom Kippur.

A packed room on Yom Kippur. Everyone is fasting. The whole congregation starts listing sins out loud. We have been guilty. We have betrayed. We have stolen. We have spoken slander. And with each word, everyone taps their chest with a fist. Here's the strange part. The gentle old man in the next row has never stolen anything in his life. And he's saying it too. We have stolen. Not I. We.
screen: `A PACKED ROOM, FASTING.` → `A FIST ON THE CHEST.` → `NOT I. WE.`

segments.voice: Ashamnu means we have been guilty. It's the first word of the short confession, and the list runs through the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to tav, one or two words per letter. We have been guilty, we have betrayed, we have robbed, we have spoken slander, and on to the end. The long confession that follows, Al Chet, is also alphabetical, and also in the plural: for the sin we have sinned before you. Every line is we. Why the alphabet? People give different reasons. One is that we've sinned with every letter, every part of speech and life. Another is that the alphabet sets a limit. The confession has an ending. You name it, and you stop. Why the plural? A teaching handed down in the name of the mystic Isaac Luria says that all Israel is like one body. If one hand does wrong, the whole body is part of it. The Talmud puts it in one line: all Israel are responsible for one another. So the old man saying we have stolen isn't lying. He's standing with the people who did, sharing the weight, and maybe admitting the ways a community lets wrongs happen. There's a model for this in the Torah. On the Day of Atonement, the high priest laid his hands on the goat and, in the old Jewish translation, would "confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel." Not his own list. Everyone's. The confession is said in each Amidah of Yom Kippur, and in many communities on ordinary weekdays too. In a room full of people, nobody has to confess alone.
screen: `ASHAMNU: WE HAVE BEEN GUILTY.` · `ALEPH TO TAV.` · `ONE BODY: RESPONSIBLE FOR EACH OTHER.` · `THE PRIEST CONFESSED FOR ALL.` · then, large: `WE, NOT I.`

segments.voice: Think of a wrong in your world that isn't only yours, something in your family, your workplace, your town, and say it quietly in the plural: we have ignored, we have been unkind. If you like, tap your chest once, lightly, and feel the weight shared, not dropped.
Ashamnu. We have been guilty. The alphabetical confession of Yom Kippur, said in the plural by everyone together.
Your line: we, not I. A week of Havdalah's trust, Elijah, Hallel, Yizkor, who by fire, Avinu Malkeinu and Ashamnu. That's six hundred thirty days.
